{"id":"persona-3tly.2","title":"PresenceLevel collapses user presence and user verification","description":"FIDO2 distinguishes two flags that mean very different things. UP, user presence, is a capacitive tap: it proves a finger touched the key, not whose. UV, user verification, is a PIN or an on-device biometric: it proves the enrolled user, to the authenticator's satisfaction.

PresenceLevel::Hardware collapses both into one value, and the enum has no way to express the difference. So a token saying hardware presence may mean a PIN was entered, or may mean anyone standing at the desk brushed the key. Those should not be the same claim to a consumer deciding whether to authorise sudo.

A bare tap is also satisfiable by a mechanical device — servo-style YubiKey touch automators exist precisely to defeat touch requirements — and by anyone who happens to be at the machine.

This is the same shape of defect as persona-okek: a level asserted more strongly than the evidence supports. The difference is that the fix is in the vocabulary rather than in the construction — PresenceLevel needs to distinguish the two, and Evidence::HardwarePresence needs to carry which flag was set.

Note SPEC-HIA's presence table describes hardware as 'FIDO2 touch, Windows Hello, TouchID, PIV PIN', which silently mixes a bare tap (FIDO2 touch) with verified interactions (PIV PIN, Windows Hello). The spec has the same conflation.","status":"open","priority":1,"issue_type":"bug","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-09-14T05:44:13.126314214Z","created_by":"agent","updated_at":"2026-09-14T05:44:13.126314214Z","labels":["presence","fido2","design"],"dependencies":[{"issue_id":"persona-3tly.2","depends_on_id":"persona-3tly","type":"parent-child","created_at":"2026-09-14T05:44:13.15279365Z","created_by":"agent","metadata":"{}"}]}

{"description":"FIDO2 distinguishes two flags that mean very different things. UP, user presence, is a capacitive tap: it proves a finger touched the key, not whose. UV, user verification, is a PIN or an on-device biometric: it proves the enrolled user, to the authenticator's satisfaction.

PresenceLevel::Hardware collapses both into one value, and the enum has no way to express the difference. So a token saying hardware presence may mean a PIN was entered, or may mean anyone standing at the desk brushed the key. Those should not be the same claim to a consumer deciding whether to authorise sudo.

A bare tap is also satisfiable by a mechanical device — servo-style YubiKey touch automators exist precisely to defeat touch requirements — and by anyone who happens to be at the machine.

This is the same shape of defect as persona-okek: a level asserted more strongly than the evidence supports. The difference is that the fix is in the vocabulary rather than in the construction — PresenceLevel needs to distinguish the two, and Evidence::HardwarePresence needs to carry which flag was set.

Note SPEC-HIRE's presence table describes hardware as 'FIDO2 touch, Windows Hello, TouchID, PIV PIN', which silently mixes a bare tap (FIDO2 touch) with verified interactions (PIV PIN, Windows Hello). The spec has the same conflation."}
